concepts.def: The poles of a magnet are the places where the magnetic forces are strongest. A bar magnet has two, a north (seeking) pole and a south (seeking) pole, one at each end.
Two like poles (north and north, or south and south) repel each other. Two unlike poles (north and south) attract each other. This rule applies to the poles of permanent magnets.

A force that acts between two objects that are not touching. The attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force: the magnets push or pull on each other across a gap.
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field. It does not need another magnet nearby, and it keeps its field when it is moved away from other magnets.

A material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field. Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction. When removed from the magnetic field an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.
The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material. The field is there whether or not anything is placed in it, and whether or not any lines have been drawn.

A material on which a magnet's field exerts a force: iron, steel, cobalt and nickel. The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction, whichever pole of the magnet is used.
The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet: the further away, the weaker the field. The field is strongest at the poles of the magnet.
The direction of the magnetic field at any point is given by the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point.
A line drawn to show the shape and direction of a magnetic field. The direction of a magnetic field line is from the north (seeking) pole of a magnet to the south (seeking) pole of the magnet.

An instrument that contains a small bar magnet, free to turn. The compass needle points in the direction of the magnetic field it sits in, so it can be used to find the direction of a field at a point.

The Earth has a magnetic field. Away from other magnets, a compass needle points in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field, which is why a compass can be used to find direction anywhere on the Earth's surface.

concepts.term: Plotting a field pattern with a compass
concepts.def: Place the magnet on paper and draw round it. Put a plotting compass near one pole and mark a dot at each end of the needle. Move the compass so the tail of the needle sits on the last dot and mark again, repeating across the paper. Join the dots into a smooth curve and add an arrow showing the direction the needle pointed. Start again from other points to build up the whole pattern.

concepts.term: Field pattern of a bar magnet
concepts.def: Smooth curved lines that leave the north pole, loop round outside the magnet and enter the south pole, each carrying an arrow from north to south. The lines are closest together at the poles, where the field is strongest, and spread further apart with distance, where the field is weaker.

concepts.term: Evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic
concepts.def: A compass needle is itself a small magnet, so it lines up with the magnetic field it is in. Away from any other magnet, and anywhere on the Earth, it still settles in a definite direction. The field turning it must therefore be produced by the Earth itself, which is evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.

mcqs.q: The north pole of one bar magnet is brought close to the north pole of another. What happens?
options: They attract each other, because magnets attract
Nothing happens until the magnets are touching
They repel only if one magnet is much stronger
They repel each other, because the poles are alike
mcqs.explain: Two like poles repel each other, so two north poles push apart.

mcqs.q: Why is the repulsion between two north poles described as a non-contact force?
options: The magnets touch each other, then spring apart
The push is really an attraction seen in reverse
The force acts through air but not through solids
The magnets push apart without ever touching
mcqs.explain: A non-contact force acts between objects that are not touching, which is exactly what happens as the two north poles are brought together.

mcqs.q: Where on a bar magnet are the magnetic forces strongest?
options: In the middle, exactly midway between the poles
At the two poles, at the ends of the magnet
At the north pole only, not at the south pole
Everywhere along the magnet, the force is equal
mcqs.explain: The poles of a magnet are, by definition, the places where the magnetic forces are strongest.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes a permanent magnet?
options: It produces its own magnetic field at all times
It becomes magnetic only when another magnet is near
It is any metal, since all metals produce fields
It is any object that a magnet is able to pick up
mcqs.explain: The specification's definition: a permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field, with no other magnet needed.

mcqs.q: A steel paperclip hangs from one pole of a bar magnet. The magnet is then taken away. What happens to the paperclip's magnetism?
options: It loses most or all of its magnetism quickly
It stays a magnet permanently from then on
It loses its magnetism only when it is heated
It keeps its magnetism and now repels other iron
mcqs.explain: The clip was an induced magnet, and an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly once out of the field.

mcqs.q: What is the key difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet?
options: Only the induced magnet is able to lose its magnetism
Only the induced magnet can both attract and repel
Only the permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field
Only the permanent magnet can be made out of steel
mcqs.explain: A permanent magnet produces its own field; an induced magnet is only a magnet while it sits in someone else's field.

mcqs.q: The north pole of a bar magnet is held close to an unmagnetised iron nail. What force acts on the nail?
options: Repulsion, because the nail is induced as a north pole
Attraction, because induced magnetism always attracts
None at all, until the nail has been magnetised
Repulsion, then attraction once the nail turns round
mcqs.explain: The nail becomes an induced magnet, and induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction.

mcqs.q: Which list contains only magnetic materials?
options: Iron, copper, cobalt and nickel
Iron, steel, cobalt and nickel
Iron, steel, aluminium and nickel
Steel, cobalt, tin and copper
mcqs.explain: These are the four magnetic materials named in the specification.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the magnetic field of a magnet?
options: The region where it exerts a force on magnetic materials
The set of lines that have been drawn around the magnet
The region right at the centre of the magnet only
The area another magnet must touch to feel a force
mcqs.explain: The field is the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.

mcqs.q: A bar magnet is brought close to a piece of unmagnetised cobalt. Which statement is correct?
options: The north pole attracts it, the south repels it
Neither pole affects it until it is magnetised
Both poles repel it, since it has no poles yet
Both poles of the magnet attract the cobalt
mcqs.explain: The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction, whichever pole is used.

mcqs.q: A plotting compass is moved from close to a bar magnet to much further away. What happens to the strength of the field at the compass?
options: It gets weaker as the compass moves away
It stays the same all round the magnet
It falls to zero outside the drawn lines
It gets stronger as the compass moves away
mcqs.explain: The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet, falling as the distance increases.

mcqs.q: On a correctly drawn field pattern of a bar magnet, where are the field lines closest together?
options: Near the middle, where the magnet is thickest
Far from the magnet, where the field is weaker
Near the poles, where the field is strongest
Evenly spaced, since the field does not change
mcqs.explain: Line spacing codes for field strength, and the field is strongest at the poles.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the magnetic field lines of a bar magnet is correct?
options: They are drawn from the south pole to the north pole
They point the way a south pole would be pushed
They run in straight lines between the two poles
They are drawn from the north pole to the south pole
mcqs.explain: The direction of a magnetic field line is from the north (seeking) pole of the magnet to the south (seeking) pole.

mcqs.q: How is the direction of a magnetic field at a point defined?
options: By the force that would act on a south pole there
By where the drawn lines are closest together
By the force that would act on a north pole there
By the way the magnet itself would move if free
mcqs.explain: The specification defines field direction as the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point.

mcqs.q: What does a magnetic compass contain?
options: A small piece of unmagnetised iron
A small bar magnet on a free pivot
A small piece of copper on a pivot
A small coil that carries a current
mcqs.explain: A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet, which is why it lines up with a field rather than merely being attracted.

mcqs.q: Well away from any other magnet, a compass needle always settles pointing the same way. What does this show?
options: The needle is pulled round by the Earth's gravity
The needle is not a magnet, it simply lines up
The Earth produces a magnetic field of its own
The needle always turns to face the nearest metal
mcqs.explain: Only a magnetic field can turn a magnet, so a consistent direction shows the Earth has a magnetic field.

mcqs.q: A student is asked to plot the magnetic field pattern of a bar magnet using a plotting compass. Which method is correct?
options: Sprinkle iron filings over the magnet and draw arrows along the lines they form
Draw a straight line from the north pole across to the south pole of the magnet
Place the compass at one point beside the magnet and record its direction only
Mark a dot at each end of the needle, move the compass on to the last dot and repeat
mcqs.explain: Stepping the compass along, dot by dot, builds a line of the field that can then be joined into a smooth arrowed curve.

mcqs.q: Which features must a correctly drawn field pattern for a bar magnet show?
options: Evenly spaced lines all round, each with an arrow on it
Curved lines with arrows running from south pole to north
Curved lines with arrows, packed closest at the poles
Straight lines joining the two poles, spaced equally apart
mcqs.explain: Spacing shows how the strength changes and the arrows show how the direction changes from point to point.

mcqs.q: How is the behaviour of a magnetic compass evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic?
options: A compass points to the magnetic rocks in the ground below
A compass lines up with a field produced inside the Earth
A compass is pulled towards the North Pole by gravity there
A compass turns because the Earth spins, dragging the needle
mcqs.explain: The needle is a magnet, so only a magnetic field can turn it; a field acting over the whole planet must come from within it.

mcqs.q: Two bar magnets are placed end to end and pull towards each other. What must be true of the facing poles?
options: They are unlike: one north and one south
They are alike, because like poles attract
One is a magnet, one an induced south pole
Both must be south poles facing each other
mcqs.explain: Two unlike poles attract each other, so an attraction between two magnets means the facing poles are unlike.
